findings.issue_text: [BUG] Update's storage-error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration instead of d.recordStorageDuration, attributing unified-storage update failures to the legacy metric. Every failed Storage.Update in mode 3 is recorded in the legacy duration histogram, so the legacy-storage SLI shows latency/errors for operations that never touched legacy storage and the storage metric under-reports failures.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's async legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration, recording legacy delete-collection results in the storage metric. Legacy DeleteCollection latency and errors are silently counted as unified-storage metrics, corrupting both histograms and making the legacy-side error rate for delete-collection unobservable.

[BUG] TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection success cases never set legacy mock expectations, so the fire-and-forget goroutine invokes Legacy.Delete/Legacy.DeleteCollection on a bare testify mock, which panics with 'mock: I don't know what to return'. The goroutine spawned by dw.Delete/dw.DeleteCollection panics asynchronously; a panic in a non-test goroutine fails the entire test binary, making these tests crash nondeterministically depending on goroutine scheduling.

[BUG] Five of the six new test functions reference the package variable p (prometheus registry) without declaring it, and the only local declaration that existed (in dualwriter_mode1_test.go line 138) is deleted in this diff; unless a package-level p exists in an out-of-diff file, the package fails to compile with 'undefined: p'. go test ./pkg/apiserver/rest/... fails to build, blocking CI entirely rather than just failing one test.

[ADVISORY] The async legacy goroutine shares the parent's mock/validation closures and the testify mock.Mock is not goroutine-safe, so concurrent Legacy calls can race with the test's own mock usage. In production the legacy write runs concurrently with the request returning; in tests, mock bookkeeping races with the test goroutine, producing flaky -race failures that do not reproduce deterministically.

[ADVISORY] The 10-second timeout context is derived from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause, but Create returns immediately, so if the server cancels the request context after responding (typical http.Server behavior), the legacy write is cancelled almost instantly. Legacy writes in mode 3 silently fail with 'legacy create timeout' whenever the inbound request finishes and its context is torn down, defeating the stated goal of writing to legacy storage; the same pattern applies to Delete (lines 138-152), Update (156-172), and DeleteCollection (176-184).

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff ever asserts the legacy-side goroutine behavior (Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection call counts or error paths), so the entire fire-and-forget legacy write path ships untested. A regression in the legacy sync (wrong object passed, dropped validation, metric mislabeling) is invisible to CI; the mislabeled recordLegacyDuration/recordStorageDuration calls in dualwriter_mode3.go are exactly the kind of defect these tests cannot catch.

[ADVISORY] Update's legacy goroutine passes the raw objInfo rather than the previously computed wrapper with the stored object, so Legacy.Update re-derives the object against legacy storage's own 'old' state. When unified storage mutated or defaulted the object during update (or the object did not exist in legacy storage), legacy storage receives a different update input than before this change, causing silent divergence between the two stores that mode 4/migration will later inherit.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's async legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration, so legacy DeleteCollection latency/failures are recorded under the storage metric. The dual-writer migration dashboards misreport legacy-store DeleteCollection results as unified-store results, hiding legacy failures during the migration window.

[BUG] Update's storage-error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) for a failed unified-storage update instead of d.recordStorageDuration. Unified-storage update failures are counted as legacy failures, corrupting both metrics series and making the storage failure rate look wrong.

[BUG] Delete's success path passes `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Delete metrics get a per-object-name `kind` label series (one series per deleted object name), causing unbounded label cardinality and making the kind dimension meaningless for deletes.

[BUG] The fire-and-forget goroutines (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) derive their 10s timeout from the request-scoped ctx, which is canceled when the HTTP handler returns, so legacy writes execute on an already-canceled context. In a real request path the async Legacy.Create/Delete/Update call fails immediately with a context-canceled error that is silently discarded (error only reflected in a metric), so legacy storage silently diverges from unified storage — the exact drift mode 3 is meant to prevent.

[BUG] Mode3 Update no longer fetches the old object or wraps objInfo (updateWrapper removed); the async legacy write passes the raw objInfo, so Legacy.Update re-resolves UpdatedObject with a different (nil/absent) old object than the one Storage.Update actually applied. Legacy storage receives an update computed against a different baseline than unified storage (or one that fails on optimistic-concurrency/resourceVersion checks), producing divergent legacy state during migration.

[ADVISORY] The same obj/object passed to the caller is concurrently read by the legacy goroutine while the caller may mutate or serialize it, with no deep copy. A data race on the returned runtime.Object between the HTTP response serialization and the async Legacy.Create/Update can produce corrupted legacy writes or race-detector failures under load.

[ADVISORY] Legacy failures in the async goroutines are never logged — the previous code logged 'unable to create/delete/update object in legacy storage', the new code only bumps a metric counter. Operators troubleshooting legacy-store divergence during migration get no log evidence of the failing writes; only an aggregate metric delta hints at the problem.

[ADVISORY] No test asserts that Mode3 actually invokes LegacyStorage (spy counts were dropped from the old commented suite), and no test exercises the async legacy path, the 10s timeout, or the metric labels. Regressions in the dual-write behavior itself — the core purpose of mode 3, e.g. legacy writes silently never happening or metrics being recorded under the wrong method name — pass CI undetected; only unified-storage behavior is covered.

[ADVISORY] The 10-second legacy timeout is hardcoded inline in four separate goroutines with per-site string literals ('legacy create timeout', 'legacy delete timeout', ...). Tuning the legacy-write budget or fixing a timeout message requires four coordinated edits; one already drifts stylistically (Update defers cancel after startLegacy), signaling the copies are diverging.

[BUG] The async legacy Update goroutine passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update instead of the previously used updateWrapper with a resolved updated object, so legacy storage receives an UpdatedObjectInfo whose old-object base was never fetched. The old code fetched `old` from Storage and wrapped objInfo so both stores wrote the same resolved object; the new code lets Legacy.Update resolve UpdatedObject against a nil/unknown old object, so the legacy store can persist a different (e.g. create-semantics) representation than the unified store, silently diverging the two backends during migration.

[BUG] On Storage.Update failure the code records the error via d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of d.recordStorageDuration, mislabeling the metric. A unified-storage update failure is counted in the legacy duration/error histogram, corrupting the mode-3 migration metrics operators rely on to decide mode promotion; the storage metric misses the failure entirely.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's async legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration for the legacy call instead of d.recordLegacyDuration. Legacy DeleteCollection latency/errors are attributed to the storage metric and legacy metrics never see DeleteCollection activity, breaking parity with the other four methods and any dashboard alerting on legacy write health in mode 3.

[BUG] Mode 3 legacy writes are now fire-and-forget goroutines with a 10s timeout and no error surfacing, retry, or reconciliation path. If a legacy write fails or times out (goroutine ctx is the request ctx of a returned request), the object exists only in unified storage while legacy reads (dashboard/playlist APIs still on legacy storage) return stale/missing data; on rollback from mode 3 to mode 2 that data is gone from the legacy system with no record that the sync failed beyond a dropped metric tick.

[ADVISORY] Create's async goroutine uses the caller's request context as parent; once the HTTP handler returns, the parent ctx is cancelled, so the 10s timeout is bounded by the request lifetime, not 10 seconds. Fast-returning requests cut legacy writes short regardless of the intended 10s budget, producing intermittent unlogged legacy-write failures in production that are invisible in code review because the timeout constant suggests otherwise.

[ADVISORY] TestMode3_Create's success case never asserts that LegacyStorage.Create was invoked (no Counts/spy assertion), so the async legacy write — the entire point of mode 3 — is untested. A regression that drops the legacy-write goroutine entirely (or makes it panic on nil legacy storage, since the mock wraps a nil LegacyStorage) passes the suite; every new mode-3 test in this diff has the same gap for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection.

[ADVISORY] TestMode3_Get constructs its own `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` while the other new mode-3 tests depend on a package-level `p` defined in a different test file, an inconsistent parallel source for the metric registry. The suite's registry setup lives in an unrelated file (dualwriter_mode1_test.go); anyone editing or deleting that file's setup silently breaks or cross-contaminates the mode-3 metric assertions, and the mode-3 tests share one registry across parallel test cases so per-test metric state is not isolated.

[ADVISORY] go.work.sum adds hashes for grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, and several otel modules that no diff in this change introduces, plus a duplicate apimachinery line already present two lines above. Dependency-hash churn unrelated to the dual-writer work rides in the same PR, making future bisects and vendor audits harder to attribute; the duplicated `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery .../go.mod` line is dead weight that any go tooling run will rewrite again.

[BUG] The async legacy Create/Update/Delete goroutines derive their context from the request ctx, so once the HTTP handler returns and the request context is canceled, the legacy write is aborted regardless of the 10s timeout, silently breaking the dual-write guarantee. Unified store gets the write, legacy store does not (context canceled mid-write), and the failure is only a metric tick — the two stores diverge silently on every fast client disconnect or short-lived request context.

[BUG] The async Update goroutine passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update, dropping the updateWrapper that previously fed the unified-store result (obj) as the updated object; legacy now recomputes the update against its own old object instead of the authoritative written object. Legacy storage stores a different version of the object than the unified store (resourceVersion / field drift), corrupting the migration invariant mode 3 exists to maintain.

[BUG] On Storage.Update failure the code records the metric with recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Storage update failures are counted as legacy failures, making the mode-3 dual-write dashboards misattribute errors and hiding the real storage error rate.

[BUG] On Storage.Create failure the code records recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Storage create failures are misattributed to the legacy metric, corrupting per-store error/success observability.

[BUG] Delete success metric passes `name` in the kind label position: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), while every other call passes options.Kind. Prometheus series for the kind label get the object name, exploding label cardinality and making per-kind delete metrics unusable.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's async goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration for the legacy delete. Legacy DeleteCollection latency/errors are reported under the storage metric, misattributing success/failure of the legacy side of the dual write.

[BUG] Delete no longer tolerates NotFound from unified storage: the previous code swallowed apierrors.IsNotFound and continued to delete from legacy; the new code returns the error immediately, so deleting an object that exists only in legacy now fails outright. During migration, objects present in legacy but not yet in unified storage become undeletable, breaking the pre-existing delete path for not-yet-migrated rows.

[BUG] Create hands the same obj pointer to the async Legacy.Create after Storage.Create has returned and possibly mutated it (e.g. set resourceVersion/UID), and the handler concurrently returns obj to the caller — an unsynchronized shared-object race. Legacy store may create an object already stamped with unified-store metadata (or race with serialization of obj in the response), producing divergent or corrupt legacy rows.

[BUG] The async Legacy.Update re-executes createValidation/updateValidation and objInfo.UpdatedObject in a detached goroutine after the request has returned, so validation now runs outside the request's auth/audit scope and any state it captures (ctx user, request-scoped values) is stale or canceled. Mutations are applied to legacy storage by a caller-validated path that no longer runs under the request's authorization context, and validation failures after the unified write are invisible to the client — the two stores diverge with no user-visible error.

[ADVISORY] Fire-and-forget goroutines with no error surface (only metrics) make mode 3's legacy divergence undetectable except via metric scraping; there is no retry, no divergence counter with identity, and no log on legacy failure. Operators relying on the dual-write phase to converge stores get silent, permanent divergence with no signal beyond a metric tick, and items missed during the window must be found by full-data comparison later.

[ADVISORY] All mode-3 tests use mock.Mock directly wrapped in typed structs (legacyStoreMock{m, l} with l == nil) and assert only return-value plumbing; no test asserts that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete is actually invoked, that the updateWrapper behavior is preserved, or that async legacy writes succeed/fail — the dual-write contract, the core of this diff, is untested. A regression that silently drops the legacy write (exactly the class of bug introduced by moving to goroutines) keeps this test suite green while production dual-write is broken.

[BUG] Mode3's contract was silently changed from synchronous dual-writes to fire-and-forget goroutines for the legacy store, with no explicit human acceptance recorded in this diff. A client that writes and immediately reads from the legacy path (or a consumer of legacy data) observes stale state after a successful 2xx response; the original mode-3 intent (write both stores before returning, log divergences synchronously) is replaced by an async best-effort copy without a documented decision, so the objective drifted during review iterations under the same 'Mode 3' label.

[BUG] The background goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create with the request-scoped ctx, which is cancelled by the server as soon as the handler returns the response. For most Create requests the legacy write fails immediately with 'context canceled' (or the 10s timeout is never reached), so mode-3 dual-writes silently diverge and the legacy duration metric records spurious failures on the happy path.

[BUG] The Update error path records d.recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration for the Storage.Update failure. Storage errors in mode-3 Update are mislabeled as legacy metrics, corrupting the dual-writer observability data that the migration plan (mode progression decisions) is based on.

[BUG] Update no longer fetches the old object and no longer wraps objInfo with updateWrapper before calling Legacy.Update — the previous mode-3 behavior of passing the reconciled updated object to the legacy store was removed without an accepted decision. The legacy store receives the raw objInfo (which may re-read state from unified storage or carry different semantics than the previously wrapped object), so legacy records can diverge from what was actually written to unified storage — an objective change hidden inside a logging/metrics refactor.

[BUG] The Delete success path passes `name` as the kind label: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), unlike every other site which passes options.Kind. The storage_duration metric gains unbounded 'kind' label values equal to object names, causing metric-cardinality explosion in Prometheus and breaking per-kind dashboards.

[ADVISORY] The Delete error path now returns the storage error unconditionally, dropping the previous IsNotFound tolerance for legacy-store errors — the old code logged legacy delete failures (including NotFound) and returned the storage result; the new code still does, but the storage error itself is no longer special-cased for NotFound, changing delete idempotency behavior. Clients retrying an already-deleted object now get an error from the unified store where the prior mode-3 semantics suppressed NotFound; behavior drift buried in the rewrite of the method during review iterations.

[ADVISORY] Legacy write goroutines are unbounded: every Create/Update/Delete spawns a goroutine holding the object and validation closures with no concurrency limit or queue, and legacy errors are only recorded as metrics, never logged (the old code logged legacy failures). Operators lose the error log signal for legacy divergence that mode-3 previously guaranteed, and under burst load goroutines pile up against a slow legacy backend; whoever investigates dual-writer drift later finds metrics but no logs.

[ADVISORY] The constant mode3Str is declared between the Mode() method and Create rather than with the other package-level mode constants, and the duplicated 'var method = ...' + log/ctx boilerplate is repeated six times across every method. Modes 1/2/4/5 receiving the same copy-pasted instrumentation in follow-up diffs will each re-introduce metric-name mistakes like the recordLegacy/recordStorage mixups in this file; a lookup-table or shared wrapper would make those sites single-sourced.

[ADVISORY] TestMode3_Create uses the package-level `p` registry while TestMode3_Get creates its own prometheus.NewRegistry() — inconsistent setup, and no test asserts that the legacy write happens at all (legacyStoreMock expectations are set but never verified via m.AssertExpectations). The rewrite to async goroutines means legacy calls are non-deterministic from the test's perspective; a regression that stops calling Legacy.Create entirely would pass these tests, so the diff's test coverage does not preserve the mode-3 contract it claims to encode.

[BUG] Client-controlled options.Kind is passed as a Prometheus label value into recordStorageDuration/recordLegacyDuration in every Mode3 handler, so any authenticated API caller can inject arbitrary label values. An attacker sending requests with unique Kind strings (e.g. 'CreateOptions{Kind: "a"+random suffix}') creates unbounded time-series cardinality in the dual-writer metrics, exhausting Prometheus/TSDB memory — a standard label-injection DoS; Kind is also interpolated into log lines enabling log-forging.

[ADVISORY] Update no longer fetches the old object and no longer wraps objInfo in updateWrapper before the legacy write, so d.Legacy.Update now receives the raw user-submitted objInfo instead of the normalized object produced by unified storage. Field stripping, defaulting, and admission normalization applied by the unified store path are bypassed in the legacy store: values the API layer pruned or defaulted can persist in legacy storage, diverging from the authoritative object and undermining any downstream security decision made from legacy data.

[ADVISORY] Legacy writes (Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection) are fired in goroutines that inherit the request context and drop all errors, so failed legacy writes are silently unrecorded in logs and aborted when the request context is canceled. An operator diagnosing dual-write drift gets no error signal — the previous code logged 'unable to create object in legacy storage'; now legacy divergence (the exact data-loss risk Mode3 introduces) happens invisibly, and any mid-request cancellation aborts the legacy replica write after the client was told the write succeeded.

[BUG] The mode-3 tests never call m.AssertExpectations() nor assert any LegacyStorage call counts, so the defining behavior of mode 3 (writing to legacy storage after the unified-store write) is never verified — the legacy mocks are set up but no assertion checks they were ever invoked. If the async goroutine that calls d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update is dropped, misrouted, or panics, every one of these tests still passes with green output; the new dual-write behavior ships unverified. This is precisely the behavior the diff changed (sync legacy writes became async goroutines) and the tests assert only the unified-storage return value.

[BUG] Every success-path test asserts only the unified-storage result while the legacy write happens in an unwaited goroutine, so the tests race: the goroutine may run after the test function returns, and any assertion added against the legacy mock (e.g. mock.AssertCalled) would be nondeterministic. Tests are flaky by construction — the asynchronous legacy write that is the core of the diff is never synchronized with the test (no channel, no clock injection, no waiting), so even a future attempt to assert legacy behavior would intermittently fail or pass vacuously depending on scheduler timing; real production timeouts (10s context.WithTimeoutCause) are also never exercised.

[BUG] TestMode3_Update's success case stubs the Legacy Update mock to return exampleObj, but the production code passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update (no updateWrapper anymore) and ignores its result — the test cannot detect whether legacy receives a stale or invalid object because it asserts nothing about the legacy call. The diff removed the updateWrapper reconciliation that previously translated the storage result for legacy storage; the legacy store now receives the caller's objInfo directly, which can write a pre-storage version of the object. No test in the diff observes the arguments passed to the legacy mock, so this behavioral regression in the diff is invisible to the suite.

[BUG] TestMode3_Create's second case ('error when creating object in the unified store fails') sets up a Legacy mock expectation but no Storage mock, then only asserts assert.Error — the test verifies that an error is surfaced but not which error, from which store, nor that legacy was (correctly) not written. The error path of the diff's changed Create branch is checked only as 'any error occurred'; a regression that returns the wrong error, writes to legacy despite storage failure, or swallows the error would pass. The wantErr branch is a bare assert.Error(t, err) with no error-content or mock-call verification.

[ADVISORY] The test table's data covers only the two paths the code already implements (storage success, storage error); there is no case for legacy-write failure, legacy-write timeout, or the error-metric recording branches the diff added. The diff added new branches (recordLegacyDuration on error paths, 10s timeout contexts, goroutine error metric recording) that no test triggers; a regression in the timeout context (e.g. wrong duration, missing cancel causing a context leak per request) or in error metric labeling would pass CI. Mirror-table parameterization covers only code-existing cases, never a spec-required case the code misses.

[ADVISORY] The success path of Create calls d.recordStorageDuration but the diff's own metric-recording helper is exercised by no assertion anywhere in the diff's tests — the mode-3 tests construct NewDualWriter with a shared package-level registry `p` and never inspect recorded metrics, so the new latency/error metric labels (mode, kind, method) are unverified. Operators relying on the new dual-writer metrics (the apparent motivation of this diff) get no test coverage that the metrics fire on success and error, or that the DeleteCollection goroutine mislabels its legacy measurement with recordStorageDuration (dualwriter_mode3.go lines ~255) — a wrong-label bug that a metric-asserting test would have caught.

[ADVISORY] TestMode3_Create asserts acc.GetResourceVersion() == "1" and assert.NotEqual(obj, anotherObj) against a mock that returns exampleObj verbatim — the assertion mirrors the canned mock value rather than testing any dual-writer behavior. These assertions are tautological with respect to the code under test: the mock returns exampleObj, so the equality assertions pass regardless of what DualWriterMode3.Create does (short of returning nil). They create false confidence that create semantics are verified when only mock pass-through is.

[ADVISORY] The new 'with dual write (etcd, mode 3)' integration test is permanently skipped via t.Skip("local etcd testing"), so of the three new mode-3 test environments added in this diff, only the file and unified-storage variants actually run. Anyone reading the test matrix believes etcd mode-3 dual-write is covered; it never executes in CI, so etcd-specific dual-write regressions surface only in production-like deployments. The skipped block is a copy of the mode-0 etcd case with no added coverage value.

[BUG] The fire-and-forget goroutine wrapping Legacy.Create inherits the HTTP request context, so the legacy-side write is aborted as soon as the request completes, silently breaking the dual-write invariant. context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) derives from the caller's request context; once the storage write returns and the handler finishes, the parent context is canceled and d.Legacy.Create fails with a cancellation error that is only counted in a metric. Legacy rows go permanently missing with no retry, reconciliation, or error surfaced to the caller — a dual-write gap that makes any later backfill/cutover from legacy data lossy.

[BUG] Mode3 Delete runs the legacy deletion in a goroutine on the (now-canceled) request context, so legacy rows are routinely left behind after unified deletion. Same parent-context cancellation problem as Create: the deferred Legacy.Delete typically never executes before the request context is torn down, leaving orphaned legacy rows that no later migration step cleans up; over time legacy and unified stores diverge and a rollback to mode 2/1 resurrects deleted playlists.

[BUG] Mode3 Update passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update instead of wrapping it with the object actually written to storage, so the two stores can persist different versions of the object. The old code resolved objInfo.UpdatedObject against the storage read and passed an updateWrapper carrying the storage result; this diff removes that wrapper, so Legacy.Update resolves objInfo against its own (possibly stale or missing) object — for forceAllowCreate it may create in legacy with different field values than unified stored, and resourceVersion conflicts cause the legacy update to fail permanently. The dual-write invariant is broken with no reconciliation path.

[BUG] Legacy.Create runs concurrently on the shared obj while the caller may serialize or mutate it, causing a data race on the object returned to the client. The goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...) after the function has returned obj to the caller; legacy storage implementations and the client serializer can mutate obj (e.g., set resourceVersion) concurrently with the response write, producing torn responses or -race failures under load.

[BUG] On the Update storage-error path, the failure is recorded with recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, mislabeling unified-storage failures as legacy failures. Dashboards and rollout gates that track storage vs legacy latency/error rates read wrong signals, so a unified-storage outage is misattributed to the legacy side and can trigger wrong mode-rollback decisions during the migration.

[BUG] The DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records its duration with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors are counted in the storage series, corrupting the migration metrics used to decide when it is safe to advance dual-writer modes.

[ADVISORY] Legacy dual-write failures in mode 3 are now completely silent (async, metric-only, no log line), whereas the previous code logged every legacy write failure. Operators migrating playlists get no log evidence that legacy writes are failing (only a counter), so divergence between the stores is discovered only when a rollback to legacy-read modes serves missing or stale data.

[ADVISORY] Removing the per-test prometheus.NewRegistry() makes TestMode1_Get share the package-level p registry, leaking metric state between tests. Tests that assert on metric values become order-dependent and can fail flakily when run with other tests that use the shared registry; parallel test runs would race on the registry.

[BUG] Legacy writes in Create are fired-and-forgotten in a goroutine whose only failure handling is a metric recording — the error is never logged and never surfaced to the user, so the API returns success while the legacy copy silently fails. In Mode 3 the contract is 'write to both storages'; a legacy Create failure (e.g. the 10s timeout, or legacy validation rejecting the mutated object) leaves the object present in unified storage but absent in legacy storage with no log line beyond a counter, so the drift is invisible and unfixable without noticing a metric.

[BUG] The Update goroutine passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update instead of the updateWrapper wrapping the resolved object that the old code built, so legacy storage re-resolves UpdatedObject from a nil/absent old object it cannot see. objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) requires the old object from unified storage; legacy storage has no access to that resolution, so legacy updates are computed from the wrong basis (or fail validation), producing divergent legacy data — a silent partial write on every Mode 3 update.

[BUG] The background legacy goroutine derives its context from the request context (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)), which is cancelled when the HTTP handler returns, so the 10-second timeout almost never protects the legacy write. The legacy Create/Update/Delete in the goroutine is aborted with 'context canceled' as soon as the response is flushed, meaning the async legacy write fails spuriously and only shows up as a failing legacy-duration metric — the dual-write guarantee is effectively best-effort-by-accident.

[BUG] On the Storage.Create error path the failure is recorded via d.recordLegacyDuration instead of d.recordStorageDuration, mislabeling storage failures as legacy failures in the metrics. Dashboards/alerts on legacy-write health in Mode 3 will fire on unified-storage failures and miss real legacy-write problems, misdirecting on-call debugging.

[BUG] On the Storage.Update error path d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) is called where the storage duration metric is intended, mislabeling the failed operation. Unified-storage update failures are counted in the legacy metric series, corrupting both metrics and any mode-migration health reporting built on them.

[BUG] The Delete goroutine swallows legacy delete errors entirely (no log, metric only), and the pre-existing behavior of ignoring apierrors.IsNotFound is gone, so a legacy delete of an already-absent object is recorded as a failure with no distinguishing signal. Every delete of an object missing in legacy storage emits a failure metric and zero diagnostic output; operators see rising legacy-delete failure rates that are partly benign NotFound noise with no way to tell real failures from expected misses.

[ADVISORY] The fire-and-forget goroutine passes the same obj and createValidation/options to Legacy.Create after Storage.Create mutated the object (resourceVersion assigned), so legacy Create receives an object already bearing unified-storage RV/metadata. Legacy storage backends that validate or set resourceVersion on create will reject or double-stamp the object, producing systematic legacy-write failures during the Mode 3 rollout that are only observable as metric counter increments.

[ADVISORY] The Update goroutine shadows ctx with the timeout-derived context but the cancel() is deferred inside the goroutine while startLegacy is timed before Legacy.Update runs — inconsistent with Create/Delete ordering (cancel declared before start, defer after), a maintenance hazard for the next edit to these four near-identical blocks. The four copy-pasted goroutine blocks (Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection) already drifted (metric function names differ, cancel placement differs); the next change to one block will likely not be replicated to the others, extending the drift already visible in this diff.

[ADVISORY] log fields read options.Kind on every method, but metav1.CreateOptions/DeleteOptions/UpdateOptions Kind is typically empty at the rest layer, so the added kind/method log labels usually log kind="". The structured logging added in this diff (its apparent purpose) is largely ineffective — dual-writer log lines cannot be filtered by kind, and metric label options.Kind will be an empty-string label value on most requests.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, DeleteCollection starts a goroutine to call d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...), but then records the result via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) instead of recordLegacyDuration. This misattributes legacy-side latency/error metrics to the storage metric, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Delete no longer tolerates NotFound from unified storage: the previous code swallowed apierrors.IsNotFound and continued to delete from legacy; the new code returns the error immediately, so deleting an object that exists only in legacy now fails outright. During migration, objects present in legacy but not yet in unified storage become undeletable, breaking the pre-existing delete path for not-yet-migrated rows.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Delete`, the old implementation explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound(err)` from `d.Storage.Delete` and still proceeded to call `d.Legacy.Delete`. The new code returns immediately on any storage error (`if err != nil { ... return res, async, err }`) and also removed the `apierrors` import/check, so a NotFound in unified storage will now fail the delete and never attempt the legacy delete. This matches the finding and is a behavior change introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Create hands the same obj pointer to the async Legacy.Create after Storage.Create has returned and possibly mutated it (e.g. set resourceVersion/UID), and the handler concurrently returns obj to the caller — an unsynchronized shared-object race. Legacy store may create an object already stamped with unified-store metadata (or race with serialization of obj in the response), producing divergent or corrupt legacy rows.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Create`, the code calls `created, err := d.Storage.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` and then starts an async goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` using the same `obj` reference (no deep copy). Many storage implementations mutate the passed-in `runtime.Object` (and often return the same pointer), meaning `obj` may alias `created` and/or be concurrently accessed while the handler returns/serializes the response. This introduces a real shared-object race and can also cause the legacy write to persist unified-store-stamped metadata.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The async Legacy.Update re-executes createValidation/updateValidation and objInfo.UpdatedObject in a detached goroutine after the request has returned, so validation now runs outside the request's auth/audit scope and any state it captures (ctx user, request-scoped values) is stale or canceled. Mutations are applied to legacy storage by a caller-validated path that no longer runs under the request's authorization context, and validation failures after the unified write are invisible to the client — the two stores diverge with no user-visible error.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Update`, the unified-store write is done synchronously, but the legacy write is moved into a detached goroutine (`go func() { ... d.Legacy.Update(...) }()`) with no error propagation/logging. Compared to the previous implementation (which precomputed `updated` once and wrapped `objInfo`), the new code passes the original `objInfo`, `createValidation`, and `updateValidation` into the async legacy call, so legacy update can re-run `objInfo.UpdatedObject(...)` and validations after the request path has already returned to the client. This makes any legacy-side validation failure invisible to the caller and can cause the two stores to diverge. It also runs using a context derived from the request context (and potentially after it’s canceled / outside normal request-scoped audit/authorization handling), which is exactly the risk described.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Fire-and-forget goroutines with no error surface (only metrics) make mode 3's legacy divergence undetectable except via metric scraping; there is no retry, no divergence counter with identity, and no log on legacy failure. Operators relying on the dual-write phase to converge stores get silent, permanent divergence with no signal beyond a metric tick, and items missed during the window must be found by full-data comparison later.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, legacy writes are moved into fire-and-forget goroutines for `Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, and `DeleteCollection` (e.g., `go func() { ... d.Legacy.Create/...; d.recordLegacyDuration(err!=nil, ...) }()`). Those goroutines do not return errors to the caller and also do not log legacy failures (they only record metrics via `recordLegacyDuration` / `recordStorageDuration`). There is also no retry logic shown. This makes legacy divergence largely invisible at request time and only observable indirectly via metrics, matching the finding’s core concern. However, this is more an operational/architecture concern than a directly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone (Mode 3 reads from Storage, so user-facing correctness may remain intact even if Legacy misses writes).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] All mode-3 tests use mock.Mock directly wrapped in typed structs (legacyStoreMock{m, l} with l == nil) and assert only return-value plumbing; no test asserts that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete is actually invoked, that the updateWrapper behavior is preserved, or that async legacy writes succeed/fail — the dual-write contract, the core of this diff, is untested. A regression that silently drops the legacy write (exactly the class of bug introduced by moving to goroutines) keeps this test suite green while production dual-write is broken.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds async legacy writes in Mode3 (e.g., Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection now call d.Legacy.* inside a goroutine with a timeout), but the new tests in pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go mostly assert only the primary return values from Unified Store operations and do not verify the legacy side-effects. The tests build legacyStoreMock{m, l} and storageMock{m, s} around a bare *mock.Mock, but they never call m.AssertExpectations(t) (or otherwise assert call counts), so a regression where the legacy write is never invoked (a key risk introduced by moving legacy writes to goroutines) would not necessarily fail these tests. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test-coverage gap for newly added nontrivial behavior rather than a directly verifiable functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Mode3's contract was silently changed from synchronous dual-writes to fire-and-forget goroutines for the legacy store, with no explicit human acceptance recorded in this diff. A client that writes and immediately reads from the legacy path (or a consumer of legacy data) observes stale state after a successful 2xx response; the original mode-3 intent (write both stores before returning, log divergences synchronously) is replaced by an async best-effort copy without a documented decision, so the objective drifted during review iterations under the same 'Mode 3' label.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows Mode3 changing legacy writes from synchronous to asynchronous: Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection now perform the Unified Store operation synchronously, then launch a `go func()` to call `d.Legacy.*` (e.g., `Create`: `go func() { ... d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`). This means the method can return success before the legacy write completes (or even starts), and because the goroutine derives its context from the request (`ctx`), it may be canceled when the request finishes, causing the legacy write to be dropped. Given Mode3’s documented intent (“writing to LegacyStorage and Storage”), this introduces a real risk of stale legacy state and missed legacy replication after a successful response.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The background goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create with the request-scoped ctx, which is cancelled by the server as soon as the handler returns the response. For most Create requests the legacy write fails immediately with 'context canceled' (or the 10s timeout is never reached), so mode-3 dual-writes silently diverge and the legacy duration metric records spurious failures on the happy path.

adjudication.rationale: In mode3 Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection, the legacy write is executed in a background goroutine that derives its context from the incoming ctx (e.g., `go func() { ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...); ... d.Legacy.Create(ctx, ...) }()`). Because `WithTimeoutCause` inherits cancellation from the parent, if the request-scoped ctx is canceled when the handler returns, the legacy call will be canceled immediately, causing the dual-write to silently skip/fail the legacy side and record failure durations even on a successful unified-store operation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The Update error path records d.recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration for the Storage.Update failure. Storage errors in mode-3 Update are mislabeled as legacy metrics, corrupting the dual-writer observability data that the migration plan (mode progression decisions) is based on.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, Update() measures the Storage.Update duration using startStorage := time.Now(), but on the Storage.Update error path it calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) instead of d.recordStorageDuration(...). This mislabels Storage failures as legacy metrics and uses the storage timing for a legacy metric.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Update no longer fetches the old object and no longer wraps objInfo with updateWrapper before calling Legacy.Update — the previous mode-3 behavior of passing the reconciled updated object to the legacy store was removed without an accepted decision. The legacy store receives the raw objInfo (which may re-read state from unified storage or carry different semantics than the previously wrapped object), so legacy records can diverge from what was actually written to unified storage — an objective change hidden inside a logging/metrics refactor.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go the Update implementation was materially changed: the previous logic fetched the current object from Storage, computed the updated object once via objInfo.UpdatedObject, and used updateWrapper to ensure both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update received a consistent, already-reconciled object. The new code directly calls d.Storage.Update(..., objInfo, ...) and then asynchronously calls d.Legacy.Update(..., objInfo, ...) without any wrapper or prior reconciliation. This objectively reintroduces the possibility that Legacy.Update re-evaluates objInfo (or reads different state) and writes something different from what Storage actually persisted, causing divergence between unified and legacy stores.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The Delete success path passes `name` as the kind label: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), unlike every other site which passes options.Kind. The storage_duration metric gains unbounded 'kind' label values equal to object names, causing metric-cardinality explosion in Prometheus and breaking per-kind dashboards.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, Delete() sets up `method := "delete"` and on the success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object `name` in the position used elsewhere for the kind label (e.g., other calls pass `options.Kind`). This will make the metric’s "kind" (or equivalent) label take arbitrary object names, creating unbounded cardinality and breaking per-kind aggregation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The Delete error path now returns the storage error unconditionally, dropping the previous IsNotFound tolerance for legacy-store errors — the old code logged legacy delete failures (including NotFound) and returned the storage result; the new code still does, but the storage error itself is no longer special-cased for NotFound, changing delete idempotency behavior. Clients retrying an already-deleted object now get an error from the unified store where the prior mode-3 semantics suppressed NotFound; behavior drift buried in the rewrite of the method during review iterations.

adjudication.rationale: In the old Mode3 Delete implementation, a NotFound from `d.Storage.Delete` was *not* suppressed: it skipped the early return but still returned `deleted, async, err` at the end, meaning the NotFound error would still be returned to the caller. The new code returns immediately on any storage error, but for NotFound the externally observed behavior (returning the storage NotFound error) is the same. The finding’s claim that prior mode-3 semantics suppressed NotFound / preserved delete idempotency is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Legacy write goroutines are unbounded: every Create/Update/Delete spawns a goroutine holding the object and validation closures with no concurrency limit or queue, and legacy errors are only recorded as metrics, never logged (the old code logged legacy failures). Operators lose the error log signal for legacy divergence that mode-3 previously guaranteed, and under burst load goroutines pile up against a slow legacy backend; whoever investigates dual-writer drift later finds metrics but no logs.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes mode-3 legacy writes to run asynchronously via `go func() { ... d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection ... }()` with a fixed 10s timeout, but there is no concurrency limiting/queuing mechanism shown, so bursts of requests will spawn many goroutines that can accumulate while the legacy backend is slow. Also, inside these goroutines legacy errors are only used to call `recordLegacyDuration(...)` (and in DeleteCollection even `recordStorageDuration(...)`) and are never logged; prior synchronous code logged legacy failures (e.g., removed `log.Error(errLeg, ...)` paths). This is a concrete, diff-grounded operational/observability regression and scalability risk, even if it may be intentional rather than a strict functional correctness break.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The constant mode3Str is declared between the Mode() method and Create rather than with the other package-level mode constants, and the duplicated 'var method = ...' + log/ctx boilerplate is repeated six times across every method. Modes 1/2/4/5 receiving the same copy-pasted instrumentation in follow-up diffs will each re-introduce metric-name mistakes like the recordLegacy/recordStorage mixups in this file; a lookup-table or shared wrapper would make those sites single-sourced.

adjudication.rationale: While the note about mode3Str placement/boilerplate is mostly maintainability, the finding’s reference to “recordLegacy/recordStorage mixups in this file” is verifiable in the diff and represents a real defect in the added instrumentation: e.g., in Create() on Storage.Create error it calls recordLegacyDuration(..., startStorage) instead of recordStorageDuration; in Update() on Storage.Update error it again calls recordLegacyDuration with the storage timer; in DeleteCollection() the legacy async path calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration; and Delete() records storage duration with `name` in the label position where other calls use `options.Kind`, indicating mislabeled metrics. These are correctness issues in the newly introduced metrics behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] TestMode3_Create uses the package-level `p` registry while TestMode3_Get creates its own prometheus.NewRegistry() — inconsistent setup, and no test asserts that the legacy write happens at all (legacyStoreMock expectations are set but never verified via m.AssertExpectations). The rewrite to async goroutines means legacy calls are non-deterministic from the test's perspective; a regression that stops calling Legacy.Create entirely would pass these tests, so the diff's test coverage does not preserve the mode-3 contract it claims to encode.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go, TestMode3_Create calls `NewDualWriter(Mode3, ls, us, p)` without creating a local registry, while TestMode3_Get explicitly does `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` and then passes that—so the setup is inconsistent in the diff. More importantly, several tests set expectations on the legacy mock (e.g., `setupLegacyFn` in TestMode3_Create / TestMode3_Update) but none of the tests call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` (or otherwise assert call counts), so a change that stops invoking the legacy methods would not necessarily fail these tests. This is especially relevant given dualwriter_mode3.go now invokes legacy writes in goroutines with timeouts, making legacy calls non-deterministic unless the tests synchronize/verify them.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Client-controlled options.Kind is passed as a Prometheus label value into recordStorageDuration/recordLegacyDuration in every Mode3 handler, so any authenticated API caller can inject arbitrary label values. An attacker sending requests with unique Kind strings (e.g. 'CreateOptions{Kind: "a"+random suffix}') creates unbounded time-series cardinality in the dual-writer metrics, exhausting Prometheus/TSDB memory — a standard label-injection DoS; Kind is also interpolated into log lines enabling log-forging.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `options.Kind` / `listOptions.Kind` being attached to logs (`WithValues("kind", options.Kind, ...)`) and passed into `recordStorageDuration`/`recordLegacyDuration` in Mode3 handlers. However, the finding’s core claim—that *API callers can arbitrarily control* these `Kind` fields to inject high-cardinality Prometheus label values—cannot be verified from the diff alone (the diff does not show how these options objects are constructed/decoded from requests, nor that `Kind` is user-supplied). Also, logging here is structured key/value logging, not string interpolation, so “log-forging” as described isn’t evidenced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Update no longer fetches the old object and no longer wraps objInfo in updateWrapper before the legacy write, so d.Legacy.Update now receives the raw user-submitted objInfo instead of the normalized object produced by unified storage. Field stripping, defaulting, and admission normalization applied by the unified store path are bypassed in the legacy store: values the API layer pruned or defaulted can persist in legacy storage, diverging from the authoritative object and undermining any downstream security decision made from legacy data.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, Update previously fetched the old object from unified storage, computed `updated := objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)`, and then used an `updateWrapper` so the legacy write would use the unified-store-produced object (`updated`/`obj`). The new code removes the `Get` + `UpdatedObject` step and calls `d.Legacy.Update(..., objInfo, ...)` directly in the goroutine, so the legacy update no longer receives the normalized object returned by unified storage. This can cause legacy storage to persist data that differs from the authoritative unified-store result (defaulting/stripping/admission effects), matching the finding’s described divergence risk.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Legacy writes (Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection) are fired in goroutines that inherit the request context and drop all errors, so failed legacy writes are silently unrecorded in logs and aborted when the request context is canceled. An operator diagnosing dual-write drift gets no error signal — the previous code logged 'unable to create object in legacy storage'; now legacy divergence (the exact data-loss risk Mode3 introduces) happens invisibly, and any mid-request cancellation aborts the legacy replica write after the client was told the write succeeded.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, legacy writes are now executed asynchronously in goroutines for `Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, and `DeleteCollection` (e.g., `go func() { ... d.Legacy.Create/... }()`), and the goroutine uses a context derived from the caller’s `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. This means if the request context is canceled, the legacy write is canceled too, while the API already returned success based on the unified store write. Additionally, the goroutines do not log legacy write errors (they only call `recordLegacyDuration(...)`), whereas the prior synchronous code logged errors like "unable to create object in legacy storage". This makes legacy-write failures and resulting drift silent and can abort legacy replication on cancellation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The mode-3 tests never call m.AssertExpectations() nor assert any LegacyStorage call counts, so the defining behavior of mode 3 (writing to legacy storage after the unified-store write) is never verified — the legacy mocks are set up but no assertion checks they were ever invoked. If the async goroutine that calls d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update is dropped, misrouted, or panics, every one of these tests still passes with green output; the new dual-write behavior ships unverified. This is precisely the behavior the diff changed (sync legacy writes became async goroutines) and the tests assert only the unified-storage return value.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go the tests set up testify/mock expectations for LegacyStorage methods (e.g., TestMode3_Create setupLegacyFn calls m.On("Create", ...), TestMode3_Update sets m.On("Update", ...)), but none of the tests call m.AssertExpectations(t) (or otherwise assert call counts). Since the production code in dualwriter_mode3.go now performs legacy writes asynchronously in goroutines, these tests can still pass even if the legacy calls never happen or don’t run before the test ends, because the tests only assert the unified-store return values and errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Every success-path test asserts only the unified-storage result while the legacy write happens in an unwaited goroutine, so the tests race: the goroutine may run after the test function returns, and any assertion added against the legacy mock (e.g. mock.AssertCalled) would be nondeterministic. Tests are flaky by construction — the asynchronous legacy write that is the core of the diff is never synchronized with the test (no channel, no clock injection, no waiting), so even a future attempt to assert legacy behavior would intermittently fail or pass vacuously depending on scheduler timing; real production timeouts (10s context.WithTimeoutCause) are also never exercised.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3` the legacy operations were changed to run asynchronously in `go func()` with a 10s `context.WithTimeoutCause` (e.g. `Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, `DeleteCollection`). In `dualwriter_mode3_test.go`, the success-path assertions only validate the returned unified-store result, and there is no synchronization/waiting mechanism to ensure the legacy goroutine has run. Some tests even set up legacy expectations via `m.On("Update"...)` / `m.On("Create"...)`, but they never call `AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled`, and even if they did, it would be nondeterministic without waiting. This is a concrete test-design gap grounded in the diff, but it does not demonstrate a production correctness defect introduced by the diff, nor necessarily current test flakiness since nothing currently asserts legacy behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] TestMode3_Update's success case stubs the Legacy Update mock to return exampleObj, but the production code passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update (no updateWrapper anymore) and ignores its result — the test cannot detect whether legacy receives a stale or invalid object because it asserts nothing about the legacy call. The diff removed the updateWrapper reconciliation that previously translated the storage result for legacy storage; the legacy store now receives the caller's objInfo directly, which can write a pre-storage version of the object. No test in the diff observes the arguments passed to the legacy mock, so this behavioral regression in the diff is invisible to the suite.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `DualWriterMode3.Update` no longer builds/uses an `updateWrapper` and instead calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` in a goroutine, i.e. it forwards the original `objInfo` rather than the object returned from `d.Storage.Update`. The updated Mode3 tests (e.g. `TestMode3_Update`) only stub `Legacy.Update`/`Storage.Update` but do not assert the legacy call’s arguments (or even that it happened), so they would not detect a change in what is written to legacy. However, whether passing raw `objInfo` is a *definite* production bug (stale/invalid object) depends on `UpdatedObjectInfo`/storage semantics not shown in the diff, so the defect claim cannot be fully verified from this patch alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] TestMode3_Create's second case ('error when creating object in the unified store fails') sets up a Legacy mock expectation but no Storage mock, then only asserts assert.Error — the test verifies that an error is surfaced but not which error, from which store, nor that legacy was (correctly) not written. The error path of the diff's changed Create branch is checked only as 'any error occurred'; a regression that returns the wrong error, writes to legacy despite storage failure, or swallows the error would pass. The wantErr branch is a bare assert.Error(t, err) with no error-content or mock-call verification.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go, TestMode3_Create’s second case (wantErr=true) only defines setupLegacyFn and omits setupStorageFn, even though DualWriterMode3.Create calls d.Storage.Create first and returns immediately on storage error (never writing to legacy). The wantErr branch only does `assert.Error(t, err)` and returns, with no assertion about which store produced the error and no mock-call verification (e.g., that legacy was not called). This is a diff-grounded test weakness/incorrect setup, not a runtime correctness bug in the production code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test table's data covers only the two paths the code already implements (storage success, storage error); there is no case for legacy-write failure, legacy-write timeout, or the error-metric recording branches the diff added. The diff added new branches (recordLegacyDuration on error paths, 10s timeout contexts, goroutine error metric recording) that no test triggers; a regression in the timeout context (e.g. wrong duration, missing cancel causing a context leak per request) or in error metric labeling would pass CI. Mirror-table parameterization covers only code-existing cases, never a spec-required case the code misses.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new nontrivial Mode3 logic branches (async legacy writes in goroutines with `context.WithTimeoutCause(..., 10s, ...)` in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection, plus new `recordStorageDuration`/`recordLegacyDuration` calls on success/error paths). The new table-driven tests in `dualwriter_mode3_test.go` primarily exercise unified-store success and unified-store error returns, and they do not trigger or assert: (a) legacy-write failure handling/metric recording inside the goroutines, (b) legacy timeout behavior, or (c) metric labeling/recording branches. No test waits for the goroutines or validates metrics, so regressions in the timeout/cancel or legacy-error metric paths could pass CI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The success path of Create calls d.recordStorageDuration but the diff's own metric-recording helper is exercised by no assertion anywhere in the diff's tests — the mode-3 tests construct NewDualWriter with a shared package-level registry `p` and never inspect recorded metrics, so the new latency/error metric labels (mode, kind, method) are unverified. Operators relying on the new dual-writer metrics (the apparent motivation of this diff) get no test coverage that the metrics fire on success and error, or that the DeleteCollection goroutine mislabels its legacy measurement with recordStorageDuration (dualwriter_mode3.go lines ~255) — a wrong-label bug that a metric-asserting test would have caught.

adjudication.rationale: The diff contains a concrete, verifiable metrics-labeling defect: in DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection the goroutine performs the legacy delete (`d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)`) but records it with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` instead of a legacy-recording helper (`d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`), so the emitted metrics are wrong for that path (pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, DeleteCollection goroutine). The finding’s point about missing metric assertions in the new mode-3 tests is also consistent with the diff, but the mislabel alone is an actual defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] TestMode3_Create asserts acc.GetResourceVersion() == "1" and assert.NotEqual(obj, anotherObj) against a mock that returns exampleObj verbatim — the assertion mirrors the canned mock value rather than testing any dual-writer behavior. These assertions are tautological with respect to the code under test: the mock returns exampleObj, so the equality assertions pass regardless of what DualWriterMode3.Create does (short of returning nil). They create false confidence that create semantics are verified when only mock pass-through is.

adjudication.rationale: In `TestMode3_Create`, the Storage mock is set up to `Return(exampleObj, nil)` and the test then asserts properties of the returned `obj` (e.g., `acc.GetResourceVersion() == "1"` and `assert.NotEqual(t, obj, anotherObj)`). Given the diff, these assertions primarily reflect the canned `exampleObj` returned by the mock rather than verifying Mode3 dual-writer semantics (e.g., that Storage is invoked first and Legacy is invoked asynchronously, or that errors/metrics/logging behave correctly). This is a test-quality issue introduced by the new test, not a functional defect in production code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new 'with dual write (etcd, mode 3)' integration test is permanently skipped via t.Skip("local etcd testing"), so of the three new mode-3 test environments added in this diff, only the file and unified-storage variants actually run. Anyone reading the test matrix believes etcd mode-3 dual-write is covered; it never executes in CI, so etcd-specific dual-write regressions surface only in production-like deployments. The skipped block is a copy of the mode-0 etcd case with no added coverage value.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go the newly added subtest `t.Run("with dual write (etcd, mode 3)", ...)` is immediately skipped via `t.Skip("local etcd testing")`, just like the existing etcd mode-0 case. From the diff, this means the new etcd mode-3 path is not exercised by default test runs/CI, so it does not actually add executable coverage for etcd-specific dual-writer mode-3 behavior despite being present in the test matrix.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The fire-and-forget goroutine wrapping Legacy.Create inherits the HTTP request context, so the legacy-side write is aborted as soon as the request completes, silently breaking the dual-write invariant. context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) derives from the caller's request context; once the storage write returns and the handler finishes, the parent context is canceled and d.Legacy.Create fails with a cancellation error that is only counted in a metric. Legacy rows go permanently missing with no retry, reconciliation, or error surfaced to the caller — a dual-write gap that makes any later backfill/cutover from legacy data lossy.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Create` (and similarly `Delete`, `Update`, `DeleteCollection`), the legacy write is moved into a fire-and-forget goroutine that calls `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the caller-provided context (`ctx` is passed through from the request and only wrapped with `klog.NewContext`). If the parent/request context is canceled when the handler completes, the derived context will be canceled too, causing `d.Legacy.Create(...)` to fail early. The goroutine does not surface or log the error (it only records a metric via `recordLegacyDuration`), so this can silently skip legacy-side writes, creating a dual-write gap with no retry/reconciliation in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Mode3 Delete runs the legacy deletion in a goroutine on the (now-canceled) request context, so legacy rows are routinely left behind after unified deletion. Same parent-context cancellation problem as Create: the deferred Legacy.Delete typically never executes before the request context is torn down, leaving orphaned legacy rows that no later migration step cleans up; over time legacy and unified stores diverge and a rollback to mode 2/1 resurrects deleted playlists.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Delete`, after successfully deleting from unified storage, legacy deletion is performed asynchronously in a goroutine using `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the request-scoped parent context (`go func() { ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...) ... d.Legacy.Delete(ctx, ...) }()`). Because this child context is derived from the request context, it will be canceled as soon as the request finishes, which can cause the legacy delete to be skipped/aborted, leaving legacy data behind. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Mode3 Update passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update instead of wrapping it with the object actually written to storage, so the two stores can persist different versions of the object. The old code resolved objInfo.UpdatedObject against the storage read and passed an updateWrapper carrying the storage result; this diff removes that wrapper, so Legacy.Update resolves objInfo against its own (possibly stale or missing) object — for forceAllowCreate it may create in legacy with different field values than unified stored, and resourceVersion conflicts cause the legacy update to fail permanently. The dual-write invariant is broken with no reconciliation path.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, `Update` now calls `d.Storage.Update(...)` and then asynchronously calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the original `objInfo` (no wrapper). The removed code previously resolved `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, oldFromStorage)` and used an `updateWrapper` so the legacy update used the same already-materialized object that was written to storage. With the new code, legacy and unified storage may each call `UpdatedObject` against different “old” objects (legacy may be stale/missing), producing different updates and breaking dual-write consistency.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Legacy.Create runs concurrently on the shared obj while the caller may serialize or mutate it, causing a data race on the object returned to the client. The goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...) after the function has returned obj to the caller; legacy storage implementations and the client serializer can mutate obj (e.g., set resourceVersion) concurrently with the response write, producing torn responses or -race failures under load.

Since `d.Storage.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` may legally mutate `obj` and/or return the same object instance (aliasing `created` with `obj`), the async `Legacy.Create` can concurrently observe/mutate the same object while the caller (e.g., response serialization) is reading it, creating a verifiable data race risk introduced by this diff.

In Mode 3 the contract is 'write to both storages'; a legacy Create failure (e.g. the 10s timeout, or legacy validation rejecting the mutated object) leaves the object present in unified storage but absent in legacy storage with no log line beyond a counter, so the drift is invisible and unfixable without noticing a metric.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Update`, the old implementation explicitly resolved the updated object once (via `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` using `d.Storage.Get`) and then used an `updateWrapper` so both Unified Storage and Legacy received the same resolved object. This means Legacy will re-run `objInfo` resolution independently (potentially against different old state), which can produce divergent updates between Unified and Legacy and silently partial/incorrect legacy writes compared to the prior behavior.
